notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if every distinct value in an array has a unique occurrence count.
Idea: Count each value's frequency and compare the number of distinct frequency values with the number of distinct input values.
Technique and why it applies: A set of frequencies detects collisions between different values' occurrence counts.
Invariant: The frequency values are unique exactly when inserting them into a set does not reduce their count.
Edge cases: Negative and positive values are both valid keys; repeated frequency counts invalidate the result.
Complexity: O(n) expected time and O(n) space.
complexity_reason: A set of frequencies detects collisions between different values' occurrence counts.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum cost to move all chips to one position when moving by two costs zero and moving by one costs one.
Idea: Count chips at even and odd positions and return the smaller count, because same-parity moves cost zero and changing parity costs one.
Technique and why it applies: Since free moves preserve parity, only chips in the minority parity group need to pay one move.
Invariant: Moving a chip by two preserves parity, so all even chips can be consolidated together and all odd chips together at zero cost.
Edge cases: Positions may be negative or positive; only parity matters; moving every chip to the cheaper parity group is optimal.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Since free moves preserve parity, only chips in the minority parity group need to pay one move.

notes:
Task and constraints: Split a balanced string into the maximum number of balanced substrings, each containing equal L and R characters.
Idea: Scan the string, add one for `L` and subtract one for `R`, and count each time the balance returns to zero.
Technique and why it applies: Greedily cutting at every zero balance creates the maximum number of balanced substrings.
Invariant: A zero balance closes a balanced prefix; closing it immediately maximizes the number of balanced pieces.
Edge cases: The input is guaranteed balanced; each segment must contain equal counts of L and R; no extra storage is needed.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Greedily cutting at every zero balance creates the maximum number of balanced substrings.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return true if all coordinate points lie on one straight line.
Idea: Use the first two points as a direction vector and verify every later point has zero cross product with that vector.
Technique and why it applies: Cross-product comparisons test all points against one common direction without floating-point slopes.
Invariant: For each point, the cross-product equality means its displacement is parallel to the reference direction.
Edge cases: The problem supplies at least two points; repeated reference points require careful handling if allowed; integer arithmetic avoids slope division.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Cross-product comparisons test all points against one common direction without floating-point slopes.

notes:
Task and constraints: Starting with a zero matrix, increment every cell in each selected row and column and count cells with odd values.
Idea: Track how many selected row increments and column increments affect each coordinate; a cell is odd exactly when its row and column increment counts have opposite parity.
Technique and why it applies: Row and column increment parities determine cell parity without simulating every matrix update.
Invariant: Each cell's value parity equals `(rowCount[i]+colCount[j]) mod 2`, so only parity of the two counts matters.
Edge cases: Repeated row or column indices toggle parity each time; matrix values start at zero.
Complexity: O(mn+q) time for q increments and O(m+n) space.
complexity_reason: Row and column increment parities determine cell parity without simulating every matrix update.

notes:
Task and constraints: Shift every grid cell k positions right in row-major order, wrapping around at the end.
Idea: Flatten row-major coordinates to an index, shift each source index by `k` modulo `m*n`, and map the result back to row and column.
Technique and why it applies: A modulo index shift implements the same wraparound as moving each row-major cell right k places.
Invariant: The destination index is `(source+k) mod totalCells`, which exactly models a right rotation of the flattened grid.
Edge cases: Large k is reduced modulo the cell count; all cells retain row-major relative cyclic order; the grid is nonempty under constraints.
Complexity: O(mn) time and O(mn) output space.
complexity_reason: A modulo index shift implements the same wraparound as moving each row-major cell right k places.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the minimum time to visit points in order when diagonal, horizontal, and vertical moves each take one second.
Idea: For each consecutive pair, add `max(abs(dx),abs(dy))` to the total travel time.
Technique and why it applies: The Chebyshev distance counts diagonal steps first and straight steps for any remaining coordinate difference.
Invariant: Diagonal moves can reduce both coordinate differences at once, so the required steps equal the larger absolute difference.
Edge cases: Points are visited in the given order; a single point needs zero time; coordinates may move in any direction.
Complexity: O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The Chebyshev distance counts diagonal steps first and straight steps for any remaining coordinate difference.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return A, B, Draw, or Pending for a valid sequence of tic-tac-toe moves.
Idea: Apply each move to the board and check its row, column, and relevant diagonal for three matching marks; if no win occurs, decide Draw versus Pending from move count.
Technique and why it applies: Checking the affected lines after each move detects a win immediately and distinguishes terminal from unfinished games.
Invariant: After every move, a winning line ends the game; otherwise a full board is a draw and an incomplete board is pending.
Edge cases: The move sequence is valid; only the last player can newly create a win; board coordinates are within 3x3.
Complexity: O(1) time and O(1) space because the board is fixed size.
complexity_reason: Checking the affected lines after each move detects a win immediately and distinguishes terminal from unfinished games.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return the product of the digits minus their sum.
Idea: Extract digits with modulo ten, multiply them into a product and add them into a sum, then return product minus sum.
Technique and why it applies: Digit extraction by remainder and integer division computes the product and sum without converting to a string.
Invariant: After each iteration, the accumulators contain the product and sum of all digits already extracted.
Edge cases: For a single digit the result is zero; zero itself has digit sum zero and digit product zero in the usual implementation.
Complexity: O(log n) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Digit extraction by remainder and integer division computes the product and sum without converting to a string.

notes:
Task and constraints: Return how many integers in the array have an even number of decimal digits.
Idea: For each number, count its decimal digits and increment the answer when the digit count is even.
Technique and why it applies: Counting decimal digits per value directly tests the required even-length property.
Invariant: The answer counts exactly the values already processed whose decimal representation has even length.
Edge cases: Single-digit values do not qualify; input values are positive under the usual constraints.
Complexity: O(n log M) time for maximum value M and O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: Counting decimal digits per value directly tests the required even-length property.
